Polis telah membuat tangkapan secara berasingan terhadap dua lelaki semalam kerana telah memuat naik hantaran berkecenderungan menghasut bagi mendatangkan penghinaan atau membangkitkan perasaan tidak setia terhadap institusi diraja.
Pengarah Jabatan Siasatan Jenayah Polis Diraja Malaysia (PDRM) Datuk Sri Mohd Shuhaily Mohd Zain berkata, suspek pertama dipercayai pemilik atau pengendali akaun Facebook Flat Earth Malaysia berusia 41 tahun.
Suspek berkenaan, jelasnya, ditangkap di Kampung Sungai Kati, Ipoh berhubung hantaran yang berbaur penghinaan terhadap institusi diraja Johor.
Sementara itu, suspek kedua, kata beliau, dipercayai pemilik atau pengendali akaun Facebook, Iman Mustaqim berusia 47 tahun.
Menurut Mohd Shuhaily, suspek itu ditangkap di kawasan Langkap kerana memuat naik hantaran mengandungi kenyataan menghina Sultan Selangor.
“Permohonan reman terhadap kedua-dua suspek di bawah Seksyen 117 Kanun Tatacara Jenayah dibenarkan selama tiga hari mulai hari ini hingga 2 September.
=========================================================================================
Sehubungan itu, orang ramai antara lain menyifatkan Wan Ahmad Fayhsal tidak peka dengan larangan penggunaan bendera dalam penghasilan logo.
Hal ini memandangkan, hanya penggunaan warna asas dan motif bendera iaitu merah, putih, biru dan kuning sahaja dibenarkan dalam gubahan logo.
“Bendera Machang ke tu?
“Siapa ajar kamu buat bendera macam tu?
“Siapa bagi kau hak untuk tukar atau ubahsuai bendera kebangsaan? Kau rakyat negara mana?” demikian antara komentar warganet.
Malah, pentadbir Facebook Komunikasi Keadilan Hulu Langat menggesa Polis Diraja Malaysia (PDRM) mengambil tindakan terhadap mana-mana yang menghina Jalur Gemilang.

𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝘀𝘁𝗮𝘁𝘂𝘁𝗼𝗿𝘆 𝗱𝗲𝗰𝗹𝗮𝗿𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝘁𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝗠𝗖𝗔 𝘀𝗶𝗴𝗻𝗲𝗱 𝗶𝗻 𝟮𝟬𝟮𝟮 𝘄𝗮𝘀 𝘁𝗼 𝘀𝘂𝗽𝗽𝗼𝗿𝘁 𝗣𝗲𝗿𝗶𝗸𝗮𝘁𝗮𝗻 𝗡𝗮𝘀𝗶𝗼𝗻𝗮𝗹

MCA President Wee Ka Siong recently said in a media interview that he did not sign a statutory declaration to support PAS President Abdul Hadi Awang as Prime Minister. This is sophistry, his cunning deception.

The SD that Wee signed was to support Muhyiddin Yassin, who was then Chairman of Perikatan Nasional, in establishing a federal government with Bersatu and PAS.

In the 19 November 2022 general election, Pakatan Harapan won 82 parliamentary seats nationwide (71 in Peninsular Malaysia), Perikatan Nasional won 74 seats (71 in the Peninsula), while Barisan Nasional secured 30 seats (23 in the Peninsula). No coalition obtained a simple majority of 112 seats.

At that point of time, Wee Ka Siong’s SD was signed to support the formation of a Perikatan Nasional government with Muhyiddin as Prime Minister.

Wee’s reasons for signing the SD were:

1. He believed the situation at the time was chaotic.
2. He adhered to the idea of “no Anwar, no DAP”, and therefore, supported Perikatan Nasional in forming the government.

If the next general election, be it in 2026 or 2027, once again sees a three-cornered fight between Pakatan Harapan, Barisan Nasional, and Perikatan Nasional, we may again see that no single coalition secures a simple majority. 

We can also be fairly certain that if history repeats, Wee Ka Siong would probably once again support Perikatan Nasional to form the government.

Wee is among the strongest advocates within Barisan Nasional for a three-cornered contest in the next general election. This is because he believes a three-way contest would allow MCA to contest more seats, not just confined to their two incumbent seats.

Since this MCA President has chosen to bring up this issue, and given that he is one of the strongest proponents of a three-cornered fight, he has to make clear to the voters whether he will support the now PAS-dominated Perikatan Nasional in forming the government should the political situation of 2022 recurs.

At least by being honest, voters can know what MCA stands for.

"PAS WAS FURIOUS UNTIL THEIR EMERGENCY MEETING. WHAT HAPPENED?"

BY LOKMAN ADAM

The emergency PAS meeting ended exactly the way many expected. All smoke, no fire. After days of dramatic warnings against Bersatu, PAS leaders suddenly went silent after gathering their top leadership behind closed doors. Malaysians were left staring at political theatre without a conclusion.

This is the problem with PAS today. The party wants to sound fierce in public but cautious in reality. They openly accuse Bersatu of betrayal, arrogance and breaking promises, yet when the moment arrives to make a hard decision, PAS retreats into silence.

That is not strength. That is political hesitation.

PAS president Abdul Hadi Awang already laid out serious accusations against Bersatu. He claimed Bersatu blocked coalition expansion, ignored agreements and damaged the spirit of cooperation within Perikatan Nasional. The Perlis Menteri Besar controversy was even cited as proof of Bersatu’s bad faith.

If those accusations are true, why is PAS still dragging its feet?

A political party that truly believes its partner is toxic should not need endless meetings and indefinite reviews. It should act decisively. Instead, PAS now looks trapped inside a relationship it no longer trusts but is too afraid to abandon.

Bersatu, meanwhile, continues behaving like a party obsessed with control and dominance. Since the beginning, Bersatu’s political style has revolved around leverage, pressure and survival tactics. The coalition was never built on mutual respect. It was built on temporary convenience and electoral desperation.

That is why PAS and Bersatu increasingly resemble toxic twins. One weaponises religious and emotional narratives while the other masters political manoeuvring and power games. Their partnership was stitched together by ambition, not sincerity.

Now both sides are exposing each other publicly. PAS complains Bersatu cannot be trusted. Bersatu sees PAS as dependent but unwilling to leave. The coalition no longer projects confidence. It projects suspicion, insecurity and internal decay.

The biggest loser in all this confusion is Perikatan Nasional itself. Elections are approaching fast, yet its own leaders cannot even provide clarity about whether the coalition still has genuine unity. Voters are expected to trust leaders who clearly no longer trust each other.

What happened after the PAS special meeting says everything. Loud accusations before the meeting. Deafening silence after the meeting. PAS wants the political mileage of attacking Bersatu without carrying the courage and consequences of making a final decision. That is not leadership. That is political limbo dressed up as strategy.

So these folks should just shut up before they open their mouth about  the problem in Negeri Sembilan or Johor state elections and call UMNO names.
They should just look at themselves  in the mirror. It's horrible.

PETALING JAYA: PAS is expected to let Perikatan Nasional (PN) go dormant without formally dissolving it as cooperation with Umno and Bersatu is no longer viewed as a viable option, according to a political scientist.

Wong Chin Huat of Sunway University said PAS now appears ready to shift course and build a new coalition with the Reset movement led by Hamzah Zainudin, as well as Pejuang and Berjasa.

He said cooperation with Umno and Bersatu was impossible as the two parties were large enough to become significant rivals, likening the three-way dynamic to rival suitors.

“The advantage of Pejuang and Berjasa is that they are small and insignificant. As such, they are likely to accept whatever PAS offers in exchange for projecting an image of Malay-Muslim unity,” he told FMT.

Wong added that such a coalition would also free PAS from negotiating seat allocations with Bersatu, while allowing its new allies to contest against Bersatu on their own terms.

He was commenting on remarks by PAS treasurer Iskandar Abdul Samad, who suggested that a coalition comprising PAS, Pejuang, Berjasa and Reset could provide the most stable platform to advance the Malay-Muslim agenda.

However, Iskandar said such cooperation would likely face attempts to undermine it, without elaborating further.

Azmil Tayeb of Universiti Sains Malaysia said that PAS sees itself as capable of operating independently, or alongside other parties or movements, having realised that losing Bersatu would not significantly affect it.

He said this was evident during the last general election (GE15), when Bersatu was shown to be heavily dependent on PAS’s grassroots machinery to remain electorally competitive.

“It would resemble the GE14 model, where PAS worked with smaller parties like Berjasa to form the Gagasan Sejahtera coalition, yet still managed to win 18 parliamentary seats at the time,” he said.

Azmil also said Umno’s preference for contesting solo, overlapping traditional seats, and a complex political history between the parties would make any post-PN cooperation difficult.

“Parti Bersama Malaysia (Bersama), meanwhile, has a different ideology because its struggle is not rooted in Malay-Islam supremacy,” he said.

Text:
No More BN, PH or PN: It’s Time for Party Bersama Malaysia 

Rafizi Ramli and Nik Nazmi have officially resigned from PKR, vacated their seats in Pandan and Setiawangsa, and taken leadership of Party Bersama Malaysia. 

This marks a bold and necessary break from the endless cycle of Malaysian politics.

Enough is enough.

For far too long, Malaysian politics has been trapped in a tired rotation between PH (DAP, PKR, AMANAH), BN (UMNO, MCA, MIC), and PN (PAS, BERSATU). 

Every election feels like a repeat: the same faces, the same coalitions, the same disappointments. 

Are you not bored? 
Are you not tired? 
Are you not disappointed?

We have enough of Anwar’s rhetoric.
We have enough of DAP’s endless drama.
We have enough of PH’s excuses.
We have enough of UMNO and BN’s corruption.
We have enough of PAS and PN’s racism, radicalism, and foolishness.

Why must the question always be “If not Anwar, then who?” — only to be answered with Muhyiddin, Hadi Awang, or Zahid Hamidi? 

At ages 78, 79, 78, and 73 respectively, these are politicians from a previous era. 

Old politics. Old mindset. 

It is time we treated political relevance with an expiry date.

We are done choosing the lesser evil. We are done debating who is the “best among the worst.”

It is time for something better.

It is time for Party Bersama Malaysia — a fresh, young, and vibrant force in Malaysian politics. 

A party that moves beyond race and religion, and focuses instead on ideas, policies, competence, and real progress. 

A party that prioritises the future over the past.

We have given BN, PH, and PN their chances. 

All have failed to deliver the Malaysia we deserve.

Today, we say NO.

No more DAP
No more PKR
No more PAS
No more UMNO
No more BN
No more PH
No more PN

Bersama Kita Bersatu
Bersama Kita Majukan Negara
Bersama Kita Melakar Sejarah Demi Masa Hadapan Malaysia Yang Lebih Baik

PETALING JAYA: Bersatu has expressed regret over remarks made by PAS president Abdul Hadi Awang against the party, saying issues involving Perikatan Nasional should be resolved within the coalition’s Supreme Council.

In a statement issued by its political bureau, Bersatu said it nevertheless sought to clarify Hadi’s remarks and avoid “misunderstandings and negative perceptions” of the coalition.

This comes after Hadi said PAS was reassessing its ties with Bersatu, including the possibility of contesting the next general election without the party led by Muhyiddin Yassin.

Regarding the Negeri Sembilan political crisis, Bersatu denied claims that it had acted unilaterally or backed down from an agreement with Umno to form a new state government.

The party said its secretary-general Azmin Ali and PAS secretary-general Takiyuddin Hassan had worked closely from the outset to manage the issue.

Bersatu said both parties had initially agreed that the state’s five PN assemblymen would cooperate with the 14 Umno assemblymen to ensure political stability.

However, it said the situation changed after Umno decided to remain with the Pakatan Harapan-led Negeri Sembilan government.

PETALING JAYA: Bersatu has dismissed speculation that the party could work with Pakatan Harapan (PH) again, saying it would not follow Umno’s path in cooperating with the ruling coalition.

Bersatu information chief Tun Faisal Ismail Aziz said there had never been any discussions within Bersatu — whether formally or informally — about rejoining PH.

Tun Faisal also said it would not make sense for Bersatu to align itself with PH once again after playing a key role in the collapse of the PH-led government in February 2020.

“Bersatu was among those that brought down the 22-month PH government, blocked Anwar Ibrahim from becoming prime minister, and removed DAP from the government,” said Tun Faisal in a statement.

“(Cooperation with PH) does not make sense.”

He also criticised Umno, claiming the party betrayed Barisan Nasional voters by supporting PH chairman Anwar to form the unity government after the 2022 general election resulted in a hung Parliament.

“At this point, there are no signs that Bersatu wants to become like Umno, which was willing to make Anwar the prime minister through deception and betrayal of BN voters’ mandate,” he said.

Speculation over Bersatu’s ties with PH surfaced following tensions between Bersatu and PAS within Perikatan Nasional. This came after PAS president Abdul Hadi Awang announced that the Islamic party might contest the next general election without its PN ally.

He cited several issues that had strained relations, including the change of Perlis’s menteri besar and Bersatu’s opposition to admitting new Malay-Muslim parties into PN, warning that “patience has its limits”.

DAP secretary-general Loke Siew Fook has since dismissed rumours of Bersatu rejoining PH.

Our politicians enjoy a luxurious retirement that keeps them firmly in the T20 category for life — even after they stop working.

This is the true meaning of being "Mahakaya". 

They serve just 3 to 5 years as clowns in the State Assembly or Parliament, and for the rest of their lives (and even for their spouses after they pass away), money flows in every month automatically through generous pensions.

Text:
The Racial Arithmetic is Brutal but Real 
Betty Teh | Malaysian Politics 

Malaysian elections are still heavily ethnicised. 

The Malay vote fractures between UMNO, Bersatu, PAS, and now potentially PKR and Bersama. The Chinese and Indian votes function largely as a defensive bloc gravitating toward whichever side appears most viable against conservative dominance. 

In this landscape, any new entrant risks being labelled a spoiler before it fields a single candidate. The cynics are already sharpening their pens. Another party, they say. Another split. Another gift to Perikatan Nasional wrapped in idealism and delivered to PAS on a silver platter. 

This fear is not irrational. 

In a First-Past-The-Post system, a 10% swing in a marginal seat is not a footnote, it is a verdict. 

Critics paint the scenario with uncomfortable precision: Bersama draws educated moderate voters from both communities who previously backed PH, the consolidated Malay Muslim right sails through the middle, and the progressive camp loses seats it could have held by simply staying together. 

The Sheraton Move trauma runs deep. Non Malay voters in particular remember watching coalitions fracture and reform with alarming frequency, each time extracting a democratic price paid by ordinary people while politicians renegotiated their positions behind closed doors. 

The instinct to consolidate to hold your nose and vote for the least bad option is not cowardice. It is hard won wisdom from a decade of watching fragmentation serve the wrong side. 

But here is what the cynics’ argument quietly assumes — that PH, left undisturbed, would have held those seats anyway. That the disillusionment driving voters toward Parti Bersama is Bersama’s creation rather than PH’s inheritance. 

That a party which failed to repeal the Sedition Act, renewed Azam Baki’s contract three times, opened criminal investigations against Bloomberg for reporting what was already in the public domain, and watched its own Youth chief call for investigations into civil society using the language of national security threats — would somehow have retained the progressive vote through sheer incumbency. 

Bersama did not create the fracture. It emerged from it. 

The split happened the moment PH chose accommodation over accountability. 

Rafizi and Nik Nazmi are not the cause of progressive exhaustion. They are its most visible symptom. 

The deeper question is whether Malaysian democracy can afford to remain hostage to racial arithmetic indefinitely. 

Every election cycle the argument is the same — not now, not this time, the stakes are too high, hold the line, we cannot risk it. 

And every cycle the parties that benefit from this logic grow more comfortable taking their voters for granted precisely because those voters have nowhere else to go. 

A captive vote is a devalued vote. The moment you guarantee your support regardless of performance, you have surrendered your leverage entirely. 

What Bersama offers whatever its electoral prospects is the restoration of that leverage. 

It tells PH that progressive voters have a choice. And parties that face genuine competition tend, over time, to govern better than those that do not. 

I joined Parti Bersama Malaysia as an ordinary member. Not because I believe it will win GE16 decisively, nobody credible is claiming that. But because I believe Malaysia needs a politics where ideas compete, where voters are not guilt tripped into perpetual loyalty to imperfect coalitions, and where the argument for change does not always have to wait for a safer moment that never comes. 

The racial arithmetic is brutal but real — and the only way to change it is to stop organising exclusively around it. 

That is what Bersama is attempting. 

Messily, imperfectly, with limited machinery and considerable courage. 

Whether it succeeds or fails, the attempt itself is necessary. A democracy that punishes people for trying to build something new is not protecting reform. It is rationing it.

Text:
MERENCANA POLITIK BARU MALAYSIA

Tindakan 5 ADUN Bersatu  dan 3 ADUN PAS di Perlis menandatangi akuan bersumpah sehingga membawa kepada pertukaran Menteri Besar amat mendukacitakan. Sepatutnya mereka membantu MB sebaiknya untuk memajukan Perlis. Malangnya mereka memilih untuk berkomplot dan menjatuhkannya.

Peristiwa ini wajar mendorong PAS untuk menilai semula kerjasama yang dibina bersama Bersatu. Pasti Bersatu juga memikirkan perkara sama. Pendekatan kepimpinan tertinggi Bersatu membenarkan rampasan kuasa berlaku boleh ditafsir bahawa mereka juga sebenarnya sudah bersedia untuk meninggalkan kerjasama dengan PAS. 

Jika PAS kekal tenang dan 'mengizinkan' rampasan kuasa itu berlaku, ia akan memberi gambaran bahawa PAS bukan parti yang mudah bertindak atas emosi. Malahan PAS mungkin akan dianggap sebuah parti yang mempunyai tahap kematangan politik luar biasa.

Namun begitu, untuk membawa perubahan besar dalam lanskap politik negara, tenang dan matang sahaja tidak mencukupi. PAS perlu dilihat sebagai sebuah parti yang penuh iltizam untuk membina harapan dan masa depan rakyat Malaysia.

PAS perlu dilihat dan boleh dirasai oleh ahlinya dan rakyat Malaysia akan kesungguhannya untuk menjadi parti yang berani, tegas dan bersungguh-sungguh dalam membenteras sistem politik semasa negara yang sarat korupsi, kronisma, nepotisma, penipuan, penindasan, penganiayaan, rasis & pengkhianatan.

Atas sebab itu, adalah amat wajar untuk PAS memberi pelajaran bermakna kepada Bersatu. Krisis Perlis adalah peluang terbaik PAS untuk menzahirkan ketegasannya dalam membina budaya politik baru buat negara -  Berdisiplin, Bersih, Berintegriti, Adil & Berwawasan.

Hari ini majoriti rakyat Malaysia khususnya orang Melayu, anak muda dan mereka yang rasional pasti akan menolak parti politik yang terkenal dengan korupsi, rasuah, kronisma, nepotisma, rasis melampau, penipuan, pengkhianatan & penganiyaan.

Perangai hodoh itu jugalah yang membuatkan tahap kepercayaan masyarakat kepada orang politik semakin hari semakin merosot. Telah tiba masanya anak-anak Malaysia terbaik memimpin negara.

PAS berpotensi untuk muncul sebagai parti yang meneraju pemulihan politik Malaysia dari krisis kepercayaan rakyat terhadap ahli dan parti politik hari ini.

Untuk itu, semua ahli politik hatta merentasi parti yang jujur, ikhlas,  bersih, berintegriti, adil & berwawasan untuk membina Malaysia baru perlu bersama. PAS boleh memainkan peranan penyatuan ini. Ia boleh dipanggil Perikatan Nasional, Muafakat Nasional, Perpaduan Nasional atau apa sahaja boleh digagaskan. Gagasan ini boleh lebih besar dari penyatuan orang Melayu sahaja. Dengan kata lain, ia boleh juga bergerak ke arah penyatuan semua kaum utama di Malysia.

Matlamat pembentukan jajaran baru berteraskan blok parti politik atau menerusi penghijrahan tokoh-tokoh (ADUN, ahli parlimen & kepimpinan) berkualiti bernaung di bawah payung besar atas agenda bersama iaitu selamatkan Malaysia wajar diusahakan secara serius.

Telah tiba masanya rakyat Malaysia bangkit memperbetulkan segala kepincangan yang berlaku dalam negara hari ini. Pilihlah pemimpin yang ikhlas dan tekun bekerja untuk rakyat dan negara. 

Jangan bimbang untuk berubah. Tinggalkan pemimpin yang korup dan sarat dengan pelbagai liabiliti. Hentikan kerakusan mereka. Hanya rakyat yang boleh melakukannnya.

Dr. Haim Hilman

‐------------------------------------------------------------

Reimagining a New Political Future for Malaysia

The recent actions of five Bersatu Assemblymen and three PAS Assemblymen in Perlis, who signed statutory declarations leading to the change of the Menteri Besar — are deeply disappointing. Instead of strengthening the state administration and supporting the leadership entrusted by the people, they chose a path that created instability and political uncertainty.

This episode should serve as a moment of reflection, not only for PAS but also for Bersatu. The apparent willingness of Bersatu’s top leadership to allow such a political manoeuvre suggests that the party itself may no longer be committed to the spirit of cooperation that once underpinned the alliance.

Many are celebrating signs that PN is fracturing, that Bersatu may no longer stand firmly with PAS. To them, it feels like a weakening of the opposition and a lesser threat from PAS. 

But there is another side that deserves calm, strategic thought. The real threat is when PAS comes into power on their own! 

PAS without coalition partners is not automatically weaker. Coalitions force compromise, moderation, and accountability. They require PAS to balance ideology with economic realities, constitutional limits, and a plural society. A fundamentalist PAS without compromises will be a bigger threat to our multiracial society then a PAS forced to work together with others. 

A PAS that no longer depends on partners has fewer reasons to explain, persuade, or restrain itself.
It will be free to posture , buy-in and appeal to radicals without consideration for others and if the ground swelled? 

The real danger is not PAS entering power when it is still dependent, when it must negotiate, compromise, and coexist.

The real danger is PAS entering power when it is strong enough to stand alone, answerable only to its own base and “acting” like a purist and theocratic without having to be real. 

History teaches us that power tested early will be shaped by restraint;  whereas power if gained after dominance is shaped by extremes and forced enforcements.

Which will be a bigger “evil”? Absolute power or compromise power? 

Politics is not just about who governs. The question is when they do, and under what constraints and restraints?

Think ! Ponder 🤔 
#######################################

Ramai sedang meraikan tanda-tanda bahawa PN semakin berpecah, dan Bersatu mungkin tidak lagi berdiri teguh bersama PAS. 

Bagi mereka, ini dilihat sebagai kelemahan pihak pembangkang dan ancaman PAS yang semakin berkurangan. 

Namun, ada satu sisi lain yang wajar difikirkan secara tenang dan strategik. Ancaman yang lebih digentari ialah apabila PAS berkuasa bersendiri tanpa gandingan kuasa.

PAS tanpa rakan gabungan tidak semestinya lebih lemah. PAS Gabungan akan memaksa kompromi, kesederhanaan dan kebertanggungjawaban. 

Ia memaksa PAS menyeimbangkan ideologi dengan realiti ekonomi, batas Perlembagaan, serta hakikat masyarakat majmuk. 

PAS yang bersifat fundamentalis tanpa kompromi sebenarnya merupakan ancaman yang lebih besar kepada masyarakat berbilang kaum berbanding PAS yang dipaksa bekerjasama dengan pihak lain.

PAS yang tidak lagi bergantung kepada rakan gabungan untuk sokongan politik akan semakin  bebas untuk menjelaskan pendirian, memujuk sokongan, tanpa kompromi atau menahan diri. 

PAS akan bebas berpostur politik, membuat naratif dan optik untuk memancing sokongan dan merayu golongan radikal tanpa perlu mengambil kira perasaan atau kepentingan pihak lain.

Bahaya sebenar bukan apabila PAS memasuki kuasa ketika mereka masih bergantung pada sokongan rakan-rakan yang memerlukan  rundingan, kompromi dan kewujudan bersama atau “win-win situation.”

Bahaya sebenar ialah apabila PAS mencapai kuasa ketika mereka cukup kuat untuk berdiri sendiri, tanpa gabungan dan cuma bertanggungjawab kepada penyokong sendiri, dan “bertindak” sebagai golongan puris tanpa perlu berpijak pada realiti pentadbiran yang sebenar. 

Sejarah mengajar kita bahawa kuasa yang diimbang, diuji lebih awal akan dibentuk oleh kawalan dan batasan; manakala kuasa yang diperoleh selepas dominasi cenderung dibentuk oleh ekstremisme dan penguatkuasaan secara paksa.

Jadi, yang manakah lebih berbahaya, apabila PAS memperolehi kuasa mutlak politik atau kuasa politik yang terikat dengan kompromi?

Politik bukan sekadar soal siapa yang memerintah tetapi bila mereka memerintah, dan samada mereka di bawah kekangan serta kawalan maupun imbangan kuasa mana,  juga amat penting.

Fikirlah ! Renungilah !

Two New Parties, Two Different Worlds — Malaysia's Political Landscape Cracks Open
Betty Teh | Malaysian Politics 
18 May 2026

On the same Sunday that Pakatan Harapan held its first convention in four years in Johor Bahru, gathering under the theme "Tekad Madani, Harapan Rakyat" to project unity ahead of GE16; two of its most prominent former ministers were in Petaling Jaya doing something the convention was specifically designed to prevent.

History, as it turns out, did not check the convention schedule.

The Method: How You Build a Party Without Building a Party

At the PJ Performing Arts Centre on Sunday 17 May 2026, Parti Bersama Malaysia founder and president Tan Gin Theam handed the party's registration certificate to Datuk Seri Rafizi Ramli and Nik Nazmi in front of more than 3,000 supporters. No new party was formed. No ROS application was filed. No years of bureaucratic purgatory endured. 

They simply took over what already existed.

Parti Bersama Malaysia also known as the Malaysian United Party, or Parti MU was registered in Penang on 2 December 2016. It was established as a third force intended to serve as a check and balance on both government and opposition. In its entire existence before Sunday, it had contested seats and lost its deposits. It was, in the most technical sense, a registered political party. And in Malaysian politics, that registration is worth more than any election result. 

This is not a new playbook. PKR itself was born from the shell of Parti Rakyat Malaysia in 1999, when Anwar Ibrahim's Reformasi movement needed a registered vehicle fast. PSM fought for ten years to get its own registration. The lesson every serious Malaysian political operator has learned is the same: do not fight the Registrar of Societies. Find someone who already won that fight and buy their house.

Rafizi and Nik Nazmi found a ten year old house in Penang for the price of a handshake and a ceremony.

Why They Did It — The Kamikaze Calculation

Rafizi called the takeover their "second kamikaze mission." "We know there is no guarantee we will succeed. We might lose our deposits in every seat and be laughed at," he said to 2,000 supporters who responded with the kind of noise that suggests they did not find it funny at all. 

"Every day people ask, what has happened? Why are Pakatan and PKR like this? Why are Pakatan betraying their core principles and repeating the same mistakes we elected them to fix? It is hard to answer," said Nik Nazmi.

Text:
Bersama and the shifting dynamics of Malaysian opposition politics 

P. Ramasamy
Chairman Urimai 
May 27, 2026

There are many political perspectives on the recent formation of Bersama (Parti Bersatu Malaysia) headed by the former deputy president of PKR Rafizi Ramli and some of his colleagues.

While the detractors are convinced that Bersama might not be too different to PKR ideologically, the supporters think that the party formed by the former minister of economy has the required traction to weaken the PH-led coalition headed by Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim.

The replacement of Rafizi as the deputy president of PKR by none other than the daughter of Anwar, Nurul Izzah Anwar, has not been well received by those who are opposed to nepotism and cronyism.

Rafizi or Bersama’s greatest political strength is none other than the lack of much-needed institutional reforms in the country.

Anwar has been playing politics with reforms by giving excuses such as the lack of consensus and others.

Of course, some detractors have posed the question to Rafizi as to what were his contributions in furthering reforms in the country.

Rafizi might not have the answer, but the fact that he was just a minister and not the prime minister must be considered.

The rise in the membership of the party is indicative of the level of dissatisfaction with the leadership of Anwar and the coalition he is heading.

Whether Bersama is able to pose a formidable challenge to PKR or the PH coalition remains to be seen.

The multiracial PKR is not the same reform-minded party as before.

Internal conflicts are haemorrhaging the party to the extent that it appears divided and disunited.

It is expected that Bersama might be able to tap into the internal dissatisfaction within PKR to attract support.

Bersama is a recent political formation; let us not underestimate the growing opposition to the administration of Anwar.

It is not Bersama alone that wants to pose a challenge to the PH ruling coalition, but also Umno/BN.

If circumstances are propitious, there is a real possibility that Umno/BN might go solo in the coming elections.

In the opposition front, all is not quiet. There might be political rumblings within PN that remain unresolved between PAS and Bersatu. 

PAS wants to accommodate the faction headed by Hamzah Zainudin that is opposed to Bersatu’s president Muhyiddin Yassin.

How such conflicts will play out remains to be seen.

Under these circumstances, Muhyiddin has strengthened his role by the formation of the broad coalition by the name of Ikatan Prihatin Rakyat (IPR).

Unlike PAS, with its feeble non-Muslim component called Dewan Himpunan Penyokong PAS (DHPP), PAS is not stupid enough to realise that the DHPP, given its meek leadership, will have little impact in drawing the support of non-Muslims in the country.

If the present conflict between PAS and Bersatu is not amicably resolved, both might go different ways in facing the elections in the country.

PAS can forget the fact that it is one of the main contenders for national power.

Under the present fluid political circumstances, there is an urgent need for parties such as the newly formed Bersama, Bersatu and others to think out of the box in order to forge a strong opposition to the present PH-led ruling coalition.

If a credible opposition front can be formed, Umno might indeed be induced to go solo.

Text:
Good afternoon 

The PMXI Fantasy League: Why Yes, Why No
By Betty Teh

Let's be honest. Anwar is 78. The "post Anwar question" is no longer whispered in policy circles, it's being openly debated at mamak stalls, in WhatsApp groups, and apparently on my Facebook comments section.

So I did what any reasonable person would do. I looked at the potential candidates and asked: why yes, why no?

Here we go.

1. Khairy Jamaluddin

Why Yes:

* Articulate, polished, looks like he actually reads the briefing notes
*. Pandemic vaccine rollout gave him genuine credibility
* Urban professionals love him. Like, really love him and I am not talking about just Kian Ming. 
* Has ministerial experience. Knows how government works.
* That podcast voice? Undeniable.

Why No:

* Just announced he's rejoining UMNO via Rumah Bangsa agenda. On March 6, 2026, after UMNO President Zahid Hamidi opened the door for "unconditional unification" of sacked members, KJ publicly declared his intent to return.
* He's even instructed his press secretary to draft the application letter. Shahril Hamdan? Not joining. "More comfortable outside politics for now."
* So KJ is back in the lion's den with Zahid, with the old guard, with all the baggage he spent years distancing himself from.
* Can he really lead reform from inside a party he was kicked out of? Or will he just be a well dressed backbencher with a podcast?
* Too elite for rural voters, too liberal for conservatives, too UMNO rooted for reformists and now actually in UMNO again, so the "independent voice" credibility takes a hit.

Verdict: Great CV. Party sorted. Identity crisis incoming.

2. Rafizi Ramli

Why Yes:

* The policy brain. Data driven. Actually reads spreadsheets.
* Positioned himself as the "conscience of Reformasi."
* Younger, reform minded voters trust him.
* Has been openly critical of the government which takes guts when your boss is the PM.
* The "ideas man" Malaysia needs.

Why No:

* Lost the PKR deputy presidency to Nurul Izzah.
* Resigned from cabinet, then spent more time criticising than building.
* Policy depth doesn't always translate to mass appeal.
* Anwar allegedly wants him out of PKR for good.
* Currently stuck in a weird family drama where he's supposed to fight the daughter but the real enemy is the father.
* Intellectual leadership inspires analysts. The rakyat? Less so.

Verdict: Would make an excellent Prime Minister's brain. Being the Prime Minister may be a different story altogether.

3. Nurul Izzah Anwar

Why Yes:

* Anwar's daughter. Political heir. Number two in PKR.
* Clean image. No corruption scandals. Actually seems to mean well.
* Has been speaking up on MACC issues even when it contradicts her father.
* A PKR MP just warned Anwar that ignoring her could risk his legitimacy.
* Popular with reformists who still believe in... reform.

Why No:

* Lost her own constituency in the last election. Let that sink in.
* Has never held a ministerial position.
* Her gender will be a disadvantage. I'm not saying it's fair but let's get real
* Perak PKR had to issue statements defending her "visibility" because people thought she'd disappeared.
* Currently trapped in "papa and mama" party nepotism narrative.
* The Sabah elections kept her busy, but did anyone notice? Apparently not.

Verdict: The heir apparent who can't inherit the throne if she can't win a seat.

4. Ahmad Samsuri Mokhtar (PAS)

Why Yes:

* Just appointed Perikatan Nasional chairman.
* Terengganu is performing well under him (yes, I checked the numbers again), shrug
* Clean image. Technocrat background. Doesn't scream "extremist."
* PAS has the most seats in PN. They want him as PM candidate.

Why No:

* Muhyiddin already said: PN chairman ≠ PM candidate.
"Not necessarily" is doing a lot of heavy lifting in that statement.
* Bersatu is clearly uncomfortable with the idea.
* PAS has a history of winning seats but failing to negotiate power.
* Still PAS. Still PAS. Still PAS.
* Analysts say PAS must be "bold" to name him. When you need to be "bold" to name your own candidate, you're already losing.

Verdict: The opposition's best bet. But "best bet" doesn't mean "winning hand."

5. Betty Teh

Why Yes:

* Has a Hollywood star. The other four? Nothing. Recognised worldwide
* Understands the fine print (even if she needs help reading it).
* Stole a meme once and got 1.4M views. That's coalition building. And meme the only thing she is capable of stealing
* Has a Meitu filter. The others don't. More beautiful than the rest. Advantage: Betty
* Not afraid to say "I want to be the most recognisable face in Malaysia." Honesty is refreshing.
* Has so many uncles following her developed a disease called Funclelitis. Survived that SHE IS A SURVIVOR! 

Why No:

Hasn't announced running yet (but neither has anyone else, technically).
May be too busy writing articles and podcasting.

Verdict: The people's choice. The only candidate with a star WHO IS A STAR LOL. Vote Betty.

Final Word

The post Anwar era will not be decided by podcasts, Twitter trends, or even policy papers. It will be decided by coalition arithmetic, party machinery, and ground sentiment.

But if I'm being honest? CAN ONLY BE ME. Click 1 to vote Betty Teh.

Make it happen. Betty Teh for PM

BERSATU is no longer in a position to control or confront PAS within Perikatan Nasional (PN), as the coalition’s internal balance of power has shifted decisively in favour of the Islamist party, political analysts say.
James Chin said Malaysian politics at the highest level is ultimately a numbers game, and the parliamentary arithmetic within PN clearly favours PAS.
“With PAS holding 43 Members of Parliament, there is no realistic scenario in which Bersatu — which has 25 MPs — can control or challenge PAS,” he said.
Chin’s remarks follow PN’s appointment of Datuk Seri Dr Ahmad Samsuri Mokhtar as chairman, a move widely seen as cementing PAS’s dominance within the opposition pact.
He noted that earlier uncertainty surrounding the political trajectory of Datuk Seri Hamzah Zainudin had contributed to internal friction within PN. However, the leadership restructuring has now clarified the coalition’s power structure.
“There was speculation about what would happen to Hamzah. That uncertainty fuelled some of the infighting. Now the picture is clearer,” Chin said.
He cautioned that Bersatu faces longer-term structural risks, warning that if Hamzah were to build political momentum independently, further defections could occur. “It is not unthinkable that Bersatu could fragment if members decide to move again,” he said, noting that the party was founded by leaders who left Umno. “There is precedent for political migration.”

PERIKATAN NASIONAL STEPPED ON THEIR OWN DEADLY TRAP

BY LOKMAN ADAM

The relationship between PAS and Bersatu has reached a dead end, with both parties now trading accusations in public.

What started as an internal leadership rift within Bersatu — fuelled by claims of two rival camps aligned to President Tan Sri Muhyiddin Yassin and his deputy Datuk Seri Hamzah Zainudin — has now spilled outward, infecting the very coalition they helped form.

Tensions between the two parties escalated sharply during the political crisis in Perlis, which saw a PAS Menteri Besar resign and be replaced by a Bersatu leader. That episode was not an isolated incident but a visible symptom of a deeper struggle for dominance within Perikatan Nasional.

The situation deteriorated further when Muhyiddin resigned as PN Chairman effective January 1, leaving the post conspicuously vacant to this day. As observers wait to see which PAS leader might be elevated to helm the opposition coalition, the problem showed no signs of ending. Instead, fresh revelations continue to surface — most recently involving Muhyiddin’s former private secretary, Datuk Dr Marzuki Mohamad.

The PAS–Bersatu saga has grown increasingly complicated when faced with real questions: who leads, who concedes, and who gets the larger share of power. When those interests no longer align, fractures appear — through public barbs, subtle jabs, and silent manoeuvres behind closed doors.

From the voters’ perspective, this prolonged conflict has triggered political fatigue. The public can no longer expect stability or clarity of direction from PN and has begun questioning the sincerity of a partnership that appears to shift with the political seasons.

This conflict has no endpoint in sight and has steadily eroded trust — not only in PAS and Bersatu, but in the very idea of their political cooperation.

It is clear that PAS and Bersatu are unable to find a mature and realistic common ground. Perhaps both will ultimately choose to go their separate ways in the interest of their own survival.

This is the consequence of power negotiations devoid of principle, partnerships lacking honesty, and a fixation on short-term political gain over long-term credibility.

Voters are tired of Perikatan Nasional's hollow rhetoric that seems to serve only itself.

A coalition built on animosity and false narratives aimed at destroying UMNO and Barisan Nasional now appears to be collapsing under the weight of its own contradictions.

Text:
No DAP, No Chinese—Yet Bersatu and PAS Still Fighting to the Death

PN keeps shouting "Melayu bersatu" (Malays united), but in the end, they're just fighting among themselves 

How do you expect the ordinary Malays at the grassroots—the ones struggling at the bottom—to trust your rhetoric about perpaduan ummah (Muslim unity) when your own leaders are stabbing each other in the back?

There's no DAP in the Perikatan Nasional (PN) coalition. Yet Bersatu and PAS are now battling fiercely to dominate one another.

Inside Bersatu, Muhyiddin, Azmin, and Hamzah are fighting to the death for control. Inside PAS, the ulama faction and the technocrats are also clashing intensely.

Bersatu even dethroned PAS in Perlis using statutory declarations (SDs). 

Now, the latest drama is PAS trying to install their own candidate to lead PN, while Muhyiddin is desperately delaying and blocking it through tactical maneuvers.

Meanwhile, both Bersatu and PAS are rejecting any grand collaboration (kolaborasi agung nasional) with UMNO. 

Akmal Saleh wants to work with PAS, but PAS refuses to cooperate with UMNO.

This is exactly what we meant when we said: don't worry if one day there's a 100% Bumiputera government—this is what will happen. SD after SD. Betrayal after betrayal. 

Everyone fighting for positions, money, and influence. All trying to dominate each other. All scrambling to grab (sakau) more for themselves.

It was never about the community. It was never truly for the race or religion they claim to champion.

We want to ask them: Even without any Chinese or DAP in the picture, you people are still fighting each other to the death. 

So after all that, everything wrong is still DAP's fault? Still the Chinese people's fault?

Every day, you tell your supporters and the rakyat at the bottom to unite for the Malays and Islam—as if you are the true warriors (pejuang) for the Melayu. 

But in reality, the top Malay leaders are at war with one another.

What is PAS's DNA? There is no loyalty. Whichever political party partners with PAS eventually ends up with problems. History has proven it time and again: They betrayed BN, Pakatan Rakyat, Barisan Alternatif, and Muafakat Nasional. 

They will surely betray Perikatan Nasional too.

And what about Bersatu's DNA? From the day the party was born, its entire mission has been betrayal. They are all traitors at heart. 

They will end up betraying PAS as well.

All of them are obsessed with power and corruption (rasuah). It was never for the rakyat, agama, or bangsa.

What about Akmal Saleh? 

He claims DAP crossed the red line by celebrating on social media over Najib's legal troubles. But he conveniently forgets that he was one of the earliest to betray Najib after GE14—demanding that Najib step down as BN and UMNO chief.

He has forgotten that it was former UMNO leaders like Mahathir and Muhyiddin who charged, investigated, and dragged Najib to court. 

He has forgotten that it was UMNO's own Prime Minister, Ismail Sabri, who ensured Najib was sent to jail. Not DAP.

Muafakat Nasional Set to Storm Back: BN-PAS Alliance Poised for 116-Seat Majority

The Muafakat Nasional alliance between Barisan Nasional (BN) and PAS could form the next federal government with a majority of 116 seats in Parliament. 

This projection is based on expected vote swings in marginal seats currently held by Pakatan Harapan (PH) and Bersatu (PN), where many Malay voters may shift support to UMNO or PAS.

Basis of the Projection and Calculation Method

This data and seat-by-seat calculation is derived from the results of the (GE15) in 2022, assuming a straight 1-on-1 contest under a revived Muafakat Nasional alliance (no three-cornered fights between UMNO/BN and PAS).

Example: Lembah Pantai (currently held by Fahmi Fadzil of PKR)

In GE15: Fahmi Fadzil (PH-PKR) won with 35,359 votes.

UMNO (BN) came second with 21,447 votes.
PAS (PN) came third with 19,098 votes.

In a Muafakat Nasional 1-on-1 scenario: PAS’s 19,098 votes would transfer/add to UMNO’s candidate, giving UMNO a combined 40,545 votes – beating PKR’s 35,359 by a majority of 5,186 votes. 

Thus, Lembah Pantai swings to UMNO.

For the rest of the seats listed, you can apply the same formula:

Identify the GE15 votes for PH/Bersatu winner vs. UMNO/BN and PAS/PN candidates.

Combine UMNO + PAS votes and compare to the winner’s tally.

Account for potential Malay voter consolidation and Bersatu seats (many won on PAS grassroots support in PN).

Seats currently held by Bersatu are particularly vulnerable, as much of their support came from PAS voters and machinery under the Perikatan Nasional banner.

Why Muafakat Nasional is a Deadly Combination:

UMNO provides strong leadership, institutional experience, and resources.

PAS supplies powerful grassroots networks, election machinery, and a loyal voter base.

This alliance stands strong on Peninsular Malaysia alone and does not rely on any pacts with Borneo-based parties (GPS, GRS, etc.) to form the federal government.

Projected Seat Distribution After the Next General Election:

PAS: Currently 43 seats → Gains at least 9 more → 52 seats

UMNO: Currently 26 seats (after deducting 7 Sabah seats, assuming total loss, leaving 19) → Adds 33 new seats → 55 seats

MCA: Currently 2 seats → Adds 5 → 7 seats

MIC: Currently 1 seat → Adds 1 → 2 seats

Total for BN + PAS (Muafakat Nasional): 116 seats – sufficient for a simple majority (112 out of 222 parliamentary seats).

Meanwhile, PH and Bersatu face significant losses:

PKR: Currently 31 → Loses 16 → 15 seats

Amanah: Currently 8 → Loses 5 → 3 seats

DAP: Currently 40 → Loses 4 in Peninsular Malaysia (excluding Sabah and Sarawak) → 36 seats

Bersatu: Currently 30 → Loses at least 18 → 12 seats

At the state level:

PAS retains control of 4 states: Perlis, Terengganu, Kelantan, Kedah.

UMNO takes over: Negeri Sembilan, Perak, Pahang, Melaka, Johor.

Muafakat Nasional conquers 9 states in total.

OPINION | Perikatan Does Not Need Another Caretaker — It Needs a Founder

What exactly is PAS’s problem with Tan Sri Muhyiddin Yassin?

Is it the issue involving his son-in-law?

Is it the numerous court cases hanging over his head?

Is it Tun Dr Mahathir’s allegation that Muhyiddin siphoned money from Bersatu?

No.

PAS’s chief problem with Muhyiddin is far simpler, and far more fundamental: under his leadership, Perikatan Nasional is losing.

Not only is Perikatan failing to win new ground, it cannot even hold on to what it already has. Election after election, by-election after by-election, the trend has been unmistakable — Perikatan is bleeding support, slowly but steadily, and the passage of time has only worsened its condition.

What alarms PAS even more is not merely the losing, but Muhyiddin’s response to the losing — or rather, the lack of it.

1) A Leader Without Urgency

Why do I say Muhyiddin does not seem concerned?

Because there is no sense of urgency about him at all.

When an organisation has been on a downward trajectory for nearly three years, one would expect its leader to be visibly agitated — pushing reforms, making drastic changes, reshuffling leadership, rethinking strategy. One would expect frustration, anger, or at the very least, urgency.

Instead, Muhyiddin remains calm. Almost serenely so.

Perikatan has gone from good to bad, and from bad to worse, yet its chairman appears entirely unperturbed. Having Muhyiddin as PN’s leader is like having the captain of a ship who remains composed and dignified even when it is obvious that the vessel is taking on water and sinking.

2) A Temperament Mismatched to the Moment

Why does Muhyiddin project this undisturbed calm?

The charitable explanation is that this is simply his nature. He may have been born with such a temperament, or cultivated it over decades in politics because he believes it projects dignity and statesmanship.

And under different circumstances, that disposition might indeed be admirable.

If Perikatan had already governed for a decade or two, delivered prosperity, stability, and public satisfaction — and Muhyiddin was merely the next custodian of an established legacy — his calm, gentlemanly demeanour might have been ideal.

In such a scenario, Muhyiddin could have played the Lee Hsien Loong role.

Lee Kuan Yew had already built Singapore. The foundations were firm, the structure complete. Lee Hsien Loong was not expected to reinvent the nation, only to preserve and manage what already existed. His calm competence was sufficient because the heavy lifting had already been done.

Similarly, had Muhyiddin succeeded Mahathir in the early 2000s, when UMNO’s legacy was still intact and governance was relatively stable, he might have performed adequately as a legacy carrier.

But that is not today’s reality.

3) Perikatan Does Not Need a Caretaker — It Needs a Founder

Perikatan Nasional does not need a legacy carrier.

It needs a legacy creator.

It needs a leader who can fight from a position of disadvantage, withstand pressure, outmanoeuvre Pakatan Harapan, and claw its way back to Putrajaya. Only after winning can Perikatan begin to think about continuity and refinement.

In short, Perikatan needs a Lee Kuan Yew, not a Lee Hsien Loong.

Just as Singapore would likely have been swallowed by Malaysia or Indonesia had it been led by Lee Hsien Loong at its most vulnerable moment, Perikatan too risks collapse if it continues to face Anwar Ibrahim and PH with a leader whose greatest strength is calm resignation.

4) The Dr Samsuri Speculation — And Why It Misses the Point

This brings us to the recent photograph that has reignited speculation over Perikatan’s future leadership.

Earlier this week, a photo surfaced showing former PN chairman Tan Sri Muhyiddin Yassin meeting Terengganu Menteri Besar Datuk Seri Dr Ahmad Samsuri Mokhtar. The image, shared on Facebook by Bachok MP Mohd Syahir Che Sulaiman — political secretary to PAS president Tan Sri Abdul Hadi Awang — was accompanied by the caption: “Alhamdulillah, insya-Allah.”

According to Mohd Syahir, the meeting took place with Hadi Awang’s blessings and was described as a “casual” encounter following Muhyiddin’s return from overseas. He declined to confirm whether it was linked to speculation that Dr Samsuri might replace Muhyiddin as PN chairman.

Nevertheless, the timing of the photo — just days before PAS is expected to hold discussions on PN’s leadership following Muhyiddin’s resignation — makes its political signalling hard to ignore.

PAS has reportedly proposed two names to replace Muhyiddin: Datuk Seri Tuan Ibrahim Tuan Man and Dr Samsuri, while Bersatu’s Datuk Seri Hamzah Zainudin has also been floated as a potential contender.

5) Replacing Muhyiddin with Dr Sam Is Going in Circles

Yet when I look at that photograph, I feel an unmistakable sense of déjà vu.

Muhyiddin and Dr Samsuri give off the same energy.

If Perikatan replaces Muhyiddin with Dr Samsuri, it risks repeating the very mistake that has paralysed it for years. Dr Samsuri may well offer Perikatan the same calmness, the same gentlemanly restraint, and ultimately, the same strategic inertia.

That is precisely what frustrated both PAS and Bersatu about Muhyiddin in the first place — to the point that they have been trying, quietly and not so quietly, to ease him out for years.

Replacing Muhyiddin with Dr Samsuri may simply condemn Perikatan to another cycle of stagnation, followed by another prolonged and awkward attempt to remove a leader who appears decent and well-meaning, but lacks the ruthlessness and fire needed to win.

Once on top, Perikatan might find it just as difficult to remove Dr Sam as it did Muhyiddin, because like Muhyiddin, Dr Sam also has a nice guy vibe. Nobody likes to be the one to remove a nice guy, because it makes you look like a nasty guy, even if the nice guy deserves to be removed, because he is a weak guy. This problem of removing a nice guy, might be why it has taken Perikatan so long to remove Muhyiddin, despite the fact that he has provided ineffective leadership for years. 

6) Insanity, the Titanic, and the Violin

Einstein famously defined insanity as doing the same thing repeatedly while expecting a different result.

Replacing Muhyiddin with Dr Samsuri fits that definition perfectly.

Perhaps, after Perikatan has won power, stabilised governance, and secured broad public approval, someone like Dr Samsuri could serve as a capable legacy carrier.

But to put him in charge now — when Perikatan must charge uphill, under siege, against a well-entrenched Pakatan Harapan — is like appointing the bandleader of the Titanic as captain. 

All that is going to happen is that the Dr Sam, like Muhyiddin, will be playing the violin calmly, as the titanic called Perikatan continues to sink to the bottom of the ocean.

PAS has signalled its readiness to assume a more dominant leadership role within Perikatan Nasional (PN) following Muhyiddin Yassin’s resignation as coalition chairman, placing the bloc in a crucial leadership transition phase.

Text:
A 100% Malay-Bumiputera Government Isn’t the End for Non-Malays – It’s the End of the Biggest Lie in Malaysian History

There’s a lot of buzz in town about the possibility of DAP pulling its support from the government. 

In this hypothetical scenario, PKR might join forces with UMNO, Bersatu, and PAS to form a 100% Malay-Bumiputera government.

Now, what about the ultra-Malay segments who might celebrate this as a victory? 

It’s an early, premature celebration by shallow-minded folks who don’t understand the laws of nature, politics, and human behavior. 

On the surface, it looks like a unified 100% Malay-Bumiputera government.

But dig deeper, and it’s actually Malay political parties restricting and counterbalancing each other’s growth. 

What does that mean? If they unite, they’re forced to maintain the status quo, benefiting the current incumbents but stifling expansion.

Let’s break down the numbers: PAS holds 43 seats, UMNO 26, Bersatu 31, and PKR 31, totaling 131 seats. But only about 100 of those are truly secure (from UMNO, Bersatu, and PAS). 

Most of PKR’s seats are in urban mixed areas that rely on DAP’s core supporter base—they might not hold all of them. 

Even if all these parties combine, they might not dethrone DAP, not because DAP is invincible, but because its urban majority seats like Bukit Bintang, Cheras, and Kepong are rock-solid. 

Even if all Bumiputera votes consolidate, they couldn’t overtake DAP in those areas.

As the Chinese proverb goes: “One mountain can have only one tiger.” 

On the surface, it’s a 100% Bumiputera government, but behind the scenes, you’re putting tigers like Anwar, Mahathir, Muhyiddin, Hadi, and Zahid in the same arena. 

It’s only a matter of time before they start clashing and eliminating each other. 

Some might ask what I mean by Malay parties restricting one another?

If the status quo remains unchallenged, it prevents UMNO from returning to its former glory—they’ll be stuck at 26 seats.

It halts PAS’s “green wave,” leaving them at 43 seats. 

This creates a stalemate and stagnation for all Malay-Bumiputera parties. How can they grow when they can’t contest against each other?

PAS also can’t push its Islamic agenda to turn the country into an Islamic state. It’s a myth that only non-Malays oppose this—the UMNO, PKR, and Bersatu Malays have different DNA, psychology, and worldviews from PAS. 

If UMNO wanted an Islamic state, they could have done it during their heyday with a two-thirds majority as Malaysia’s largest undisputed party.

What PAS fails to understand is that not all Malays share their religious views on politics and administration.

Sooner or later, these parties will try to dominate one another. Each will plot to become the No. 1 Malay party. 

If Hamzah and Muhyiddin can fight within the same party, why is it abnormal for rival parties to scheme for ultimate dominance?

For stability, they’ll need the 56 MPs from Borneo. If they abandon this block, it’s risky—the 56 could align with DAP’s solid 40 seats and Amanah’s 8 to form a new government anytime. 

With 56 from Borneo versus PAS’s 43, Bersatu’s 31, PKR’s 31, and UMNO’s 26, Borneo becomes the kingmaker in this coalition. The moderates and progressives will call the shots.

This is what true Bumiputera check-and-balance looks like: parties counter-influencing and restricting each other. 

PAS won’t be able to ban alcohol, not because of DAP or non-Malay MPs, but because the Borneo Bumiputera won’t allow it—doing so would collapse GPS in Sarawak. That’s why a PAS candidate in Sabah even lodged a report denying plans to ban alcohol.

Not only is this their ceiling since they can’t contest each other, but it also limits their growth and puts everything in stalemate.

Yet UMNO won’t stay silent for long—their entire DNA is rooted in feudal elitism and a dominance mindset. They can’t accept being the smallest Malay party at just 26 seats.

And since non-Bumiputera are out of the government, those seats are no longer a conflict of interest. Non-Bumiputera will no longer be the election scapegoat, punching bag, or weaponized issue.

By then, it’ll be Bumiputera versus Bumiputera, outcompeting each other: left vs. right, conservative vs. progressive, religion-ahead-of-race vs. race-ahead-of-religion, B40 vs. M40 and T20, and the list goes on.

It’ll still be Bumiputera vs. Bumiputera, driven by the laws of human nature, politics, greed, dominance, power, and money.

As for PKR? There’s nothing to celebrate. Their 31 mixed urban seats are the most fragile and vulnerable in this combo, likely making them the smallest party in the Bumiputera coalition. 

It’ll also mark the end of any future prime minister from PKR. With non-Bumiputera out of the equation, whoever rises to the top in each Bumiputera party automatically wins big.

So, each party will see fierce internal killings to climb the ladder—just like UMNO in its glory days, or what’s happening in Bersatu now.

Everyone fighting for positions, candidacies, and more, because internal victory means a shot at PM. It’ll create a Game of Thrones among the Bumiputera parties.

And it won’t stop at the top. Once the non-Malays are no longer in the cabinet or government, the real war will begin over every single slice of the pie:

Which party controls which GLCs and their multi-billion-ringgit empires

Who gets the powerful minister portfolios
who heads the government agencies, statutory bodies, and regulators

All the way down to who becomes Ketua Kampung, penghulu, JKKK chairs, and every small contract and perk that comes with it.

When the “enemy” (non-Malays) is removed from the equation, the knives will turn inward even faster—pure Bumiputera musical chairs with real money, real power, and real blood.

What do non-Bumiputera have to lose? We already have nothing to begin with, always relying on ourselves. Even having our own race in the cabinet changes little—we’re still blamed and used as punching bags by aspiring politicians and parties.

And Here’s the Biggest Silver Lining Most People Miss

When the non-Malays are completely out of the government, the real true colours of Malay politicians will finally be exposed – not to us, but to their own community.

For decades, the narrative has been drilled into the Malay heartland: “Melayu terancam! Islam terancam! The Chinese are the root of your poverty!” They were told the enemy is the non-Malays – that if only we remove the non-Malays, everything will be fair, just, and prosperous for the Malays.

But the moment a 100% Bumiputera government is formed, that entire lie collapses in plain sight.

The ordinary kampung folk, the B40 Malays, the PAS supporters, the Perikatan die-hards – they will finally see with their own eyes:

The rich and elite Malays will keep getting richer.

The poor Malays will stay poor, or get even poorer.

Government projects, contracts, GLCs, and billions in wealth will still flow to the same handful of elite Malay families, cronies, and political warlords – just like before.

Their own leaders will stop fighting for them. Why? Because there is no longer a “non-Malay enemy” to rally against. No more “Cina yang halang kita!” to shout from the stages. When the votes are already 100% locked in, what slogan is left? 

Sooner or later, the realisation will hit like a thunderbolt: “Rupa-rupanya selama ini kita dipergunakan sahaja. Kita dijadikan senjata untuk lawan orang bukan Melayu, supaya segelintir ahli politik Melayu boleh naik kuasa dan kaya raya untuk diri dan keluarga mereka sendiri.

Rupa-rupanya ini bukan perjuangan bangsa dan agama – ini perjuangan pangkat, jawatan, wang, dan kemewahan peribadi.”

Even the most hardcore PAS supporters will wake up: “Rupa-rupanya 100% kerajaan Melayu-Bumiputera pun hudud tak dapat, negara Islam pun tak jadi. Sebelum ini kita ingat orang bukan Melayu yang halang – rupanya bukan!”

That moment of mass awakening among the Malay grassroots will be the most powerful, most irreversible change of all. The spell will be broken forever.

And that, ironically, might be the greatest gift a DAP withdrawal could ever give to this country – forcing the Malay community to finally see their real oppressors have never been the non-Malays sitting in Putrajaya. 

The real oppressors have always been wearing the same songkok and speaking the same language as them.

So let them have their 100% Malay-Bumiputera Government if they want it so badly.

It won’t destroy the non-Malays. 

It will destroy the biggest lie they’ve been feeding their own people for seventy years.

Itu bukan perpaduan ummah. Itu perpaduan sementara elit-elit Melayu yang nak sakau habis-habisan atas nama Melayu dan Islam.

Their 31 mixed urban seats are the most fragile and vulnerable in this combo, likely making them the smallest party in the Bumiputera coalition. It’ll also mark the end of any future prime minister from PKR. With non-Bumiputera out of the equation, whoever rises to the top in each Bumiputera party automatically wins big. So, each party will see fierce internal killings to climb the ladder—just like UMNO in its glory days, or what’s happening in Bersatu now. Everyone fighting for positions, candidacies, and more, because internal victory means a shot at PM. It’ll create a Game of Thrones among the Bumiputera parties. And it won’t stop at the top. Once the non-Malays are no longer in the cabinet or government, the real war will begin over every single slice of the pie: Which party controls which GLCs and their multi-billion-ringgit empires Who gets the powerful minister portfolios who heads the government agencies, statutory bodies, and regulators All the way down to who becomes Ketua Kampung, penghulu, JKKK chairs, and every small contract and perk that comes with it. When the “enemy” (non-Malays) is removed from the equation, the knives will turn inward even faster—pure Bumiputera musical chairs with real money, real power, and real blood. What do non-Bumiputera have to lose? We already have nothing to begin with, always relying on ourselves. Even having our own race in the cabinet changes little—we’re still blamed and used as punching bags by aspiring politicians and parties. And Here’s the Biggest Silver Lining Most People Miss When the non-Malays are completely out of the government, the real true colours of Malay politicians will finally be exposed – not to us, but to their own community. For decades, the narrative has been drilled into the Malay heartland: “Melayu terancam! Islam terancam! The Chinese are the root of your poverty!” They were told the enemy is the non-Malays – that if only we remove the non-Malays, everything will be fair, just, and prosperous for the Malays. But the moment a 100% Bumiputera government is formed, that entire lie collapses in plain sight. The ordinary kampung folk, the B40 Malays, the PAS supporters, the Perikatan die-hards – they will finally see with their own eyes: The rich and elite Malays will keep getting richer. The poor Malays will stay poor, or get even poorer. Government projects, contracts, GLCs, and billions in wealth will still flow to the same handful of elite Malay families, cronies, and political warlords – just like before. Their own leaders will stop fighting for them. Why? Because there is no longer a “non-Malay enemy” to rally against. No more “Cina yang halang kita!” to shout from the stages. Rupa-rupanya ini bukan perjuangan bangsa dan agama – ini perjuangan pangkat, jawatan, wang, dan kemewahan peribadi.” Even the most hardcore PAS supporters will wake up: “Rupa-rupanya 100% kerajaan Melayu-Bumiputera pun hudud tak dapat, negara Islam pun tak jadi. Sebelum ini kita ingat orang bukan Melayu yang halang – rupanya bukan!” That moment of mass awakening among the Malay grassroots will be the most powerful, most irreversible change of all. The spell will be broken forever. And that, ironically, might be the greatest gift a DAP withdrawal could ever give to this country – forcing the Malay community to finally see their real oppressors have never been the non-Malays sitting in Putrajaya. The real oppressors have always been wearing the same songkok and speaking the same language as them. So let them have their 100% Malay-Bumiputera Government if they want it so badly. It won’t destroy the non-Malays. It will destroy the biggest lie they’ve been feeding their own people for seventy years. Itu bukan perpaduan ummah. Itu perpaduan sementara elit-elit Melayu yang nak sakau habis-habisan atas nama Melayu dan Islam.

Ruang diberikan pada umno akan ada "time line"nya.
Sekurang kurangnya DSZH kini sudah ada mandat partinya

Kita akan mempastikan 126 kerusi yg telah dikenalpasti akan menjadi milek Muafakat ini,belum termasuk kerusi di Sarawak yg tentunya turut di undang nanti.

Bahtera tetap belayar,tapi ruang lebih banyak penumpang dengan destinasi yg sama masih terbuka.

Text:
MUHYIDDIN’S QUIET EXIT: WHEN THE GENERAL LEAVES THE BATTLEFIELD AND HANDS OVER THE MAP

THE SOUND OF A DOOR CLOSING—SOFTLY

There was no thunder. No screaming press conference. No flying keris.
Just a door closing with the politeness of a man who knows exactly where the exits are.

When Muhyiddin resigned—effective January 1, 2026—it did not feel like defeat. It felt like choreography. Like a chess piece sliding into place while everyone else was busy arguing about the rules of the game.

Generals followed. Titles evaporated. Secretaries vanished. The tent looked intact, but the poles were quietly removed. And suddenly, Perikatan Nasional was standing—upright, yes—but wobbling like a wardrobe missing its back panel.

⸻

THE CHESS MOVE THAT TRAPS THE BISHOP

This was never a rage-quit. This was strategy dressed as resignation.

By stepping aside, Bersatu didn’t abandon PN. It gift-wrapped it—and handed it to PAS. With a bow. And a smile. And absolutely no receipt.

For years, PAS had complained—loudly, consistently, with religious fervour—that PN was “controlled by Bersatu.” That they were merely passengers, not drivers. That the steering wheel was elsewhere.

Now the steering wheel is theirs.

And suddenly, the excuses evaporate like morning mist under harsh daylight.

⸻

THE DOG THAT FINALLY CAUGHT THE CAR

PAS has long claimed to have the strongest machinery.
The biggest membership.
The most disciplined grassroots.
The most prepared leaders.

Excellent.

The stage is now empty. The spotlight unforgiving. The microphone live.

There is no more villain named Bersatu to blame.
No more whispered complaints about being sidelined.
No more dreams of sneaking back to Muafakat Nasional like an ex texting at 2 a.m.

This is leadership without disclaimers.

The dog has caught the car.
Now it must decide whether to drive—or be dragged.

⸻

CORNERED BY THEIR OWN NARRATIVE

PAS now finds itself in a beautifully cruel dilemma.

To leave PN would be to confess what critics have long alleged:
that loyalty lasts only until a better ladder appears.

To stay means something far more dangerous:
governing.
Not preaching. Not posturing. Not praying for opponents to fall.

Leading.

Budgets. Policies. Accountability. Decisions that cannot be footnoted with verses when they go wrong.

This is no longer about who controls PN.
This is about whether PAS can.

⸻

PERLIS: THE CRACK THAT BECAME A FAULT LINE

The Perlis episode was not a footnote—it was a preview.

A Bersatu Menteri Besar.
PAS sidelined.
Trust eroded.
Smiles that didn’t reach the eyes.

For PAS, Perlis felt like betrayal. For Bersatu, it was just politics doing what politics always does—moving the pieces that are easiest to move.

And now, with Bersatu stepping back, PAS inherits not just the throne—but the mess beneath it.

⸻

QUNUT NAZILAH AND THE BOOMERANG EFFECT

Perhaps the bitterest irony of all is this:

After months of praying for others to stumble,
it is their own alliance that is losing its footing.

Politics has a cruel sense of humour.
Like gravity, it doesn’t care about intention.

What you throw upward eventually returns—often with interest.

⸻

THE ANGELIC SILENCE OF AI

If artificial intelligence were watching this, it would blush.

No algorithm could have plotted this with such elegance:
Resign quietly.
Trigger a leadership vacuum.
Force your ally to step forward.
Remove all alibis in one move.

Compared to this, machines look naive.
Humans, once again, outperform technology—especially in self-sabotage.

⸻

ANWAR STANDS. OTHERS UNRAVEL.

While this quiet implosion unfolds, one figure remains standing—largely untouched by the debris.

PN reshuffles. Leaders resign. Alliances tremble.
Yet elsewhere, stability looks boring—and therefore effective.

It turns out chaos is not contagious when you refuse to host it.

⸻

THE STEERING WHEEL AND THE DEAD END

Muhyiddin walked away clean.
No blood. No bruises. No public humiliation.

PAS now grips the steering wheel of PN with both hands.

But the road ahead is narrow, unlit, and suspiciously quiet.

So the final question lingers—not shouted, but whispered:

Does PAS actually want to lead?
Or does it merely want to be the driver who proves—spectacularly—that passion without navigation takes you straight into a wall?

History, as always, is sharpening its pencil.

PN BERPEGANG KEPADA DASAR DAN PRINSIP "NO ANWAR, NO DAP"

1. Pada 21 November 2022, pada jam 2 petang, hanya ada seorang Ahli Parlimen yang telah menerima cukup SD seperti yang dititahkan oleh YDPA untuk menjadi PM10 dan membentuk kerajaan (115 SD Sokongan daripada Ahli Parlimen yang lain), iaitu Tan Sri Muhyiddin Yassin. Anwar Ibrahim hanya mempunyai 81 SD.

2. Bagaimanapun hak Perlembagaan Persekutuan Tan Sri Muhyiddin telah dinafikan.

3. PM10 dan kerajaan PH-BN hari ini adalah hasil penipuan dan manipulasi Zahid Hamidi dan pengkhianatan undi pengundi-pengundi BN dan undi pengundi-pengundi PH.

4. Penjelasan Datuk Dr Marzuki Mohamad mengenai keputusan isu Kerajaan Perpaduan adalah tepat kerana BERSATU dan Pas masih berpegang teguh kepada dasar No Anwar, No Dap ini. Ia dibuat secara bersama oleh Tan Sri Muhyiddin dan Tan Sri Tuan Guru Hj Hadi Awang di Istana Negara atas prinsip ini.

Akmal Saleh’s Big Lie Exposed: UMNO Lost Malays Long Before DAP – Thanks to Your Own Corruption & Arrogance

Akmal Saleh, listen up and listen hard—you're peddling a load of half-baked lies that stink of desperation. 

It's not DAP that's costing UMNO Malay support; it's your party's own rotten history of corruption, blatant racism, and insufferable arrogance that's driven you straight into the gutter. 

At your precious Pemuda UMNO convention, you paraded "facts" claiming UMNO lost Malay votes after teaming up with DAP. 

What a joke—that's not the truth; that's a pathetic half-truth designed to dodge accountability.

Let's slap some real numbers in your face.

UMNO once commanded a whopping 75% Malay support. 

In GE14—without a whiff of DAP—your support cratered to 45%. 

Then GE15 rolls around, still no DAP in sight, and it plunges further to 35%. 

Now, after partnering with DAP, you're whining about 27%? 

That's a measly 8% drop. 

But wake up, Akmal: Before DAP ever entered the picture, you'd already hemorrhaged a massive 40% from 75% to 35%. 

That's your own self-inflicted disaster, not DAP's fault. 

And that 55% of your core UMNO supporters who bolted to PN in GE15? 

They didn't flock to DAP—they ditched you for your rivals. DAP gained zilch from your implosion.

Now you're bleating about losing rural support? 

Spare us the crocodile tears. 

Is this your way of admitting Zahid Hamidi is a total failure as Menteri Kemajuan Desa dan Wilayah? 

Rural development and kampung welfare fall squarely on his shoulders, not a single DAP minister's. 

Those rural seats didn't go to DAP—they were snatched by PAS and Bersatu. 

And here's the killer question, Akmal: Do you seriously think cozying up to PAS now will let UMNO claw back those seats? 

Hell no—the incumbents will cling to them like glue. 

It's only through the Madani coalition—with DAP in it—that UMNO has any shot at reclaiming them from PAS and Bersatu. 

Proof? 

Post-GE15, with DAP on board, you crushed the by-elections in Pelangai, Mahkota, Ayer Kuning, and Nenggiri with overwhelming majorities. 

Shoving the blame for your epic failures onto DAP isn't just irresponsible—it's gutless and utterly illogical.

Let's not forget who the real backstabbers are. 

It was PAS that betrayed UMNO, ditching Muafakat Nasional to slither into PN with Bersatu. Not DAP. 

For 33 months under PN, PAS propped up that regime while they poached your members, schemed to dissolve UMNO, froze your party accounts, and dragged your leaders through the courts like criminals. Not DAP. 

But under Madani—with DAP in the mix—Zahid got his DNAA, Rosmah walked free, and cases against Tok Mat and LCS were buried, all investigations that festered under PN's watch. 

Funny how that works, huh?

Then you have the audacity to demand a MN revival so "Malay states" like Kedah, Kelantan, and Terengganu can "develop," claiming development's only pouring into Johor, Penang, and Klang Valley. 

What a brazen distortion. 

DAP's been in power for barely three years—it's UMNO and PN's Malay-led governments that squandered nearly 70 years failing to lift those states out of poverty. 

Under Madani, the annual budgets for Kelantan, Kedah, and Terengganu dwarf what's given to Penang. 

And why do Penang, Johor, KL, and Selangor thrive? 

Not because of some magical government handout—it's the progressive, driven societies there fueling their own economies. 

Forced, artificial "development" flops like Forest City every time. 

So own it, Akmal: It's Malay leadership and society that's let those states rot, not DAP.

Crunch these numbers, since you love "facts".

There are 5,229,000 Malays in the SG4 states (Kedah: 1,803,000; Kelantan: 1,935,000; Terengganu: 1,236,000; Perlis: 255,000).

But dwarfing that? 

9,722,000 Malays in Selangor (4,153,000), Perak (1,530,000), Negeri Sembilan (761,000), Pulau Pinang (736,000), and Johor (2,542,000). 

Federal allocations to Kedah, Kelantan, and Terengganu already outstrip the rest—no issue there. 

But the second aid trickles to Penang, your walaun PN cronies erupt in outrage, even though Penang pumps among the highest GDP and revenue into the nation while getting the skimpiest allocations. 

Why the selective rage? 

Why act like there are no Malays in Penang? Those 736,000 Malays aren't real? No PAS members, supporters, or voters there? Only SG4 Malays count as "pure"?

This is peak hypocrisy from you walaun types.

You abandon your hometowns, dump your parents and grandparents in backwardness, and flock to developed states like KL, Selangor, Johor, and Penang to chase jobs and prosperity. 

Every five years, you crawl back to vote in PAS administrations that perpetuate poverty and underdevelopment in your birth states, then return to leech off the progress in non-PAS territories.

And when aid flows to those thriving states—where you live, work, and eat—you screech like hypocrites, pretending you don't benefit. What kind of twisted logic is this? 

You smear these places as capitalist dens of liberalism, vice, entertainment, and un-Islamic filth, accuse the ruling parties of every sin under the sun—yet you happily soak up their advancements and amenities. 

You vote PAS back home to keep it poor and regressive, while refusing to live there yourself. 

Demanding handouts for states you won't even stay in?

Pathetic. 

Grow a spine, Akmal—face your party's mess instead of scapegoating DAP. Your downfall is all on you.
